warmup.q: Seven cold starts each wire the same moving-day crew, once with the generated component and once with a reflection container, on a busy machine. Which difference do you expect to stay the same from run to run?
options: The time of the whole JVM run
None of them: everything jumps around on a busy machine
warmup.why: Timings depend on what else the machine is doing; between our runs they moved by about a third, though the generated side won every time. The classes a program loads depend only on the code it runs, so the count was the same in every run: 817 for the generated component and 1,059 for reflection. When a machine is noisy, count something before you time it.

opening:
Picture two crews arriving at two houses at seven in the morning. The first crew follows a sheet written the night before and starts carrying boxes. The second crew first reads every name tag on the pavement, works out who needs whom, and only then lifts anything. Both houses get moved. One crew starts later, and you'd like to know by how much.

The last two lessons wrote the plan during the build and taught it to refuse a broken plan. The easy trap now is to believe that this is faster without measuring it, or to measure only the part that's tiny.

In this sitting we'll race the generated component against a reflection container from a cold start and count the classes each one loads. Then we'll let the truck's slow GPS wait until it's needed, watch one edit go through KSP's incremental log, and meet the real tools. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two crews at two houses. The crew with the sheet written the night before was wired two to three times sooner, loaded 242 fewer classes, and never read an annotation on the day.

That closes Part 5. It began with a helper who reads the labels on sealed boxes and writes new cards. The capstone turned those cards into a plan that the build checks before anyone lifts a box.

In your own code, find one thing that reads annotations at start-up. Could its answer be written down during the build?

That ends the course. From here, take one program you know well and try one tool from each Part on it.

sections.h: Race them from cold: wiring time, start-up and classes loaded
sections.html:
First, the words in one breath. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs processors, plug-ins for the build that read your declarations and write new code. Java has had the same kind of plug-in since Java 6, the annotation processors that javac runs, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do that job for Kotlin code. Our component is the class our processor generates to build the graph: every object of the moving day, and who needs whom. It hands each object its dependencies, the objects it needs, through its constructor, which is dependency injection by constructor injection. Each line of the plan is a binding. A singleton is built once per component, anything else on each request, and each class has a generated factory that calls its constructor.

Now the race. StartupRace in the lesson 3 app starts a fresh JVM for every run, seven runs for each way of wiring the same crew. In each JVM, WiringProbe wires the crew one way and asks for the moving day twice, timing each step with System.nanoTime():

Java
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent();   // builds every singleton, in order
long t1 = System.nanoTime();
MovingDay day = plan.movingDay();                              // returns a field
long t2 = System.nanoTime();
// the other way: ReflectionContainer c = new ReflectionContainer(RouteModule.INSTANCE);
//                MovingDay day = c.get(MovingDay.class);      // reads the notes, builds everything
Kotlin
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
val plan = GeneratedMovingDayComponent()                       // builds every singleton, in order
val t1 = System.nanoTime()
val day = plan.movingDay()                                     // returns a field
val t2 = System.nanoTime()
// the other way: val c = ReflectionContainer(RouteModule)
//                val day = c.get(MovingDay::class.java)       // reads the notes, builds everything

The parent times the whole JVM run, and -Xlog:class+load, a JVM switch that logs every class as it's loaded, counts the classes. Both ways build the same crew: each probe's line ends with the plan's first line, Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway. Make your guess for the wiring ratio before you read on. On this machine, four cores with a load average around 5 from other builds, the race printed:

7 cold starts each, medians (a busy machine: compare the two rows, not the numbers with yours)
               create   first get   second get   JVM run  classes  proxy classes  annotations
generated    25.53 ms     0.00 ms     0.000 ms    181 ms      817              0            0
reflection   50.92 ms    21.02 ms     0.002 ms    256 ms     1059              6            4

The generated component does all its work in create: its constructor builds every singleton in order, so the first movingDay() only returns a field. Add create and first get together, and it's 25.5 ms against 71.9 ms, about 2.8 times faster. The whole JVM run was 75 ms shorter. An earlier run, at a higher load, gave 17.6 against 46.3 ms and 139 against 192 ms, and the Java twin's run gave 32.1 against 66.6 ms. So the times moved by a third from run to run, and the ratio stayed between 2 and 3. The class counts didn't move at all.

What are the 242 extra classes? About forty come from java.lang.reflect, much of it the JDK's proxy machinery. Six are proxy classes it generated while the program ran, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 to jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5, to stand for annotations being read. Others parse the generic signature Lazy<GpsUnit> out of the class file. And four are the annotation classes themselves. The generated component never loads Inject, Singleton, Named or Provides at all. The sticky notes did their job in the build and stayed there.

Once wired, the two are equally quick: the second request costs a few microseconds or less either way. Fifty milliseconds won't matter to a program that starts once a week. They matter to one that starts often, like a command-line tool, or a test suite that builds a fresh component for every test. And this crew has eight classes, where a real program has hundreds.

Reflection pays for the wiring at every start. Generated wiring pays once, in the build.

Look at the generated create time again. It builds everything at once, including parts nobody needs at seven in the morning. The truck's GPS is one of them.

try.title: Run the cold-start race
steps: Write down your guess: how much faster will the generated component wire the crew, and how many extra classes will reflection load?
Run StartupRace from labs/. It starts fourteen small JVMs, one after another, and prints one row per way of wiring.
Run StartupRaceJava, the same race with Java calling the same generated component and the same container.
Run StartupRace again with -Pargs=3 added (three starts each). Which columns moved, and which didn't?

code.title: StartupRace.kt
code.html: package workbench.injector.app.l03 import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path /** * Cold starts, measured: runs WiringProbe in a fresh JVM, [runs] times for each way of wiring the same crew, * with -Xlog:class+load, and prints the medians. * ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l03.StartupRaceKt */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val runs = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 7 val ways = listOf("generated", "reflection") val results = ways.associateWith { mutableListOf<Run>() } repeat(runs) { for (way in ways) results.getValue(way) += probe("workbench.injector.app.l03.WiringProbeKt", way) } println("$runs cold starts each, medians (a busy machine: compare the two rows, not the numbers with yours)") println("%-11s %9s %11s %12s %9s %8s %14s %12s".format( "", "create", "first get", "second get", "JVM run", "classes", "proxy classes", "annotations")) for (way in ways) { val r = results.getValue(way) println("%-11s %6.2f ms %8.2f ms %9.3f ms %6d ms %8d %14d %12d".format(way, median(r.map { it.createUs }) / 1000.0, median(r.map { it.firstUs }) / 1000.0, median(r.map { it.secondUs }) / 1000.0, median(r.map { it.wallMs }), median(r.map { it.classes.toLong() }), median(r.map { it.proxyClasses.toLong() }), median(r.map { it.annotationClasses.toLong() }))) } Path.of("build/startup-race").toFile().deleteRecursively() } /** * One cold start: the probe's own timings, the JVM's run time, and what -Xlog:class+load counted: every class, * the proxy classes java.lang.reflect.Proxy made while the program ran (package jdk.proxy*), and the * annotation classes (the sticky notes) that had to be loaded. */ class Run(val createUs: Long, val firstUs: Long, val secondUs: Long, val wallMs: Long, val classes: Int, val proxyClasses: Int, val annotationClasses: Int) fun probe(mainClass: String, way: String): Run { val dir = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("build/startup-race")) val log = dir.resolve("$way.log").also { Files.deleteIfExists(it) } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val command = listOf(java, "-Xlog:class+load:file=$log", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), mainClass, way) val builder = ProcessBuilder(command).redirectErrorStream(true) builder.environment().remove("JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS") // keep the child JVM plain val started = System.nanoTime() val process = builder.start() val output = process.inputStream.bufferedReader().readText() process.waitFor() val wallMs = (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000 val line = output.lines().first { it.startsWith("probe ") } fun field(name: String) = Regex("$name=(\\d+)").find(line)!!.groupValues[1].toLong() val loaded = Files.readAllLines(log).filter { "[class,load]" in it }.map { it.substringAfter("[class,load] ") } Files.delete(log) return Run(field("create"), field("first"), field("second"), wallMs, loaded.size, proxyClasses = loaded.count { it.startsWith("jdk.proxy") }, annotationClasses = loaded.count { it.startsWith("workbench.injector.annotations.") }) } fun median(values: List<Long>): Long = values.sorted()[values.size / 2]

alt.html: package workbench.injector.app.l03; import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.ToLongFunction; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * The Java twin of StartupRace: the same cold starts, with WiringProbeJava in each fresh JVM. * ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l03.StartupRaceJava */ public class StartupRaceJava { record Run(long createUs, long firstUs, long secondUs, long wallMs, long classes, long proxyClasses, long annotationClasses) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int runs = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 7; Map<String, List<Run>> results = new LinkedHashMap<>(); for (String way : List.of("generated", "reflection")) results.put(way, new ArrayList<>()); for (int i = 0; i < runs; i++) { for (String way : results.keySet()) results.get(way).add(probe(way)); } System.out.println(runs + " cold starts each, medians (a busy machine: compare the two rows, not the numbers with yours)"); System.out.printf("%-11s %9s %11s %12s %9s %8s %14s %12s%n", "", "create", "first get", "second get", "JVM run", "classes", "proxy classes", "annotations"); for (var entry : results.entrySet()) { List<Run> r = entry.getValue(); System.out.printf("%-11s %6.2f ms %8.2f ms %9.3f ms %6d ms %8d %14d %12d%n", entry.getKey(), median(r, Run::createUs) / 1000.0, median(r, Run::firstUs) / 1000.0, median(r, Run::secondUs) / 1000.0, median(r, Run::wallMs), median(r, Run::classes), median(r, Run::proxyClasses), median(r, Run::annotationClasses)); } Files.deleteIfExists(Path.of("build/startup-race")); } static Run probe(String way) throws IOException, InterruptedException { Path dir = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("build/startup-race")); Path log = dir.resolve(way + "-java.log"); Files.deleteIfExists(log); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); ProcessBuilder builder = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xlog:class+load:file=" + log, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.injector.app.l03.WiringProbeJava", way) .redirectErrorStream(true); builder.environment().remove("JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS"); // keep the child JVM plain long started = System.nanoTime(); Process process = builder.start(); String output = new String(process.getInputStream().readAllBytes()); process.waitFor(); long wallMs = (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000; String line = output.lines().filter(l -> l.startsWith("probe ")).findFirst().orElseThrow(); List<String> loaded = Files.readAllLines(log).stream().filter(l -> l.contains("[class,load]")) .map(l -> l.substring(l.indexOf("[class,load] ") + 13)).toList(); Files.delete(log); return new Run(field(line, "create"), field(line, "first"), field(line, "second"), wallMs, loaded.size(), loaded.stream().filter(c -> c.startsWith("jdk.proxy")).count(), loaded.stream().filter(c -> c.startsWith("workbench.injector.annotations.")).count()); } static long field(String line, String name) { Matcher m = Pattern.compile(name + "=(\\d+)").matcher(line); if (!m.find()) throw new IllegalStateException(line); return Long.parseLong(m.group(1)); } static long median(List<Run> runs, ToLongFunction<Run> f) { return runs.stream().mapToLong(f).sorted().toArray()[runs.size() / 2]; } }

try.expect: Two rows. Your times will differ from the ones above, but the generated row should win on create plus first get and on JVM run, with first get near 0.00 ms because its constructor already built everything. The class counts should hardly move between runs: about 817 against 1,059 (the Java twin loads a couple fewer), 0 against 6 proxy classes and 0 against 4 annotation classes. second get is tiny for both.

sections.h: The GPS can wait: Lazy<T> and () -> T
sections.html:
The truck's GPS takes a while to switch on, because it has to find the satellites first. In the demo app, GpsUnit's constructor sleeps for 300 ms to stand in for that wait, a delay chosen for teaching. With the plan as it was, the component's constructor would build the GPS along with the truck. Every start would pay those 300 ms, even on a day the truck never asks for directions.

Lazy injection fixes that. The truck asks for Lazy<GpsUnit> instead of GpsUnit. That's a box that builds its contents the first time someone opens it with .value, and hands back the same contents after that. Provider injection is its sibling. The packer asks for () -> TapeRoll, a function that hands out one more roll on every call. In the moving-day picture, the GPS is on call and comes when it's first needed, and every room gets a fresh roll of tape:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a Supplier, which the component makes build the GPS only once
public class Truck {
    private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gps;
    @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { this.gps = gps; /* ... */ }
    public String directions() { return gps.get().directionsTo("the new house"); }
}

public class Packer {
    private final Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape;                     // one more roll on every get()
    @Inject public Packer(Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape) { this.newTape = newTape; }
    public String pack(String room) { return room + " packed with tape roll #" + newTape.get().getNumber(); }
}
Kotlin
@Singleton
class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) {
    fun directions(): String = gps.value.directionsTo("the new house")   // switched on here, once
}

class Packer @Inject constructor(private val newTape: () -> TapeRoll) { // one more roll on every call
    fun pack(room: String): String = "$room packed with tape roll #${newTape().number}"
}

The processor changes in two of the KSP track's five moves. In the Read move, requestOf unwraps the type a parameter asks for: Lazy<GpsUnit> becomes (LAZY, GpsUnit), and () -> TapeRoll, whose class is kotlin.Function0, becomes (PROVIDER, TapeRoll). The key is the type inside, so every check from lesson 2 still works. Forget the GPS's @Inject, and the build says MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs GpsUnit: nobody provides GpsUnit., on the truck's gps parameter.

In the Write move, a singleton that someone asks for lazily is held in a Lazy of its own, and each request gets the expression for its kind:

Java
// The same lines in Java, written by a javac processor; memoize() is a small generated helper
private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gpsUnit = memoize(GpsUnitFactory::create);  // built on the first get()
private final Truck truck = TruckFactory.create(driver, gpsUnit);
private Packer newPacker() { return PackerFactory.create(this::newTapeRoll); }
Kotlin
private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() }      // built on the first .value
private val truck: Truck = TruckFactory.create(driver, gpsUnit)
private fun newPacker(): Packer = PackerFactory.create({ newTapeRoll() })
asked for as gpsUnit (singleton, held in a Lazy) truck (singleton, built at once) newTapeRoll (no @Singleton)
the type itself gpsUnit.value truck newTapeRoll()
Lazy<T> gpsUnit lazyOf(truck) lazy { newTapeRoll() }
() -> T { gpsUnit.value } { truck } { newTapeRoll() }

Kotlin's lazy { } is safe with threads by default: its mode is SYNCHRONIZED, so the body runs once even if two threads open the box at the same moment. The app shows the result:

crew ready after 109 ms, GPS switched on: 0
Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway
the family takes the back roads
kitchen packed with tape roll #1
pantry packed with tape roll #2
bedroom packed with tape roll #3
GPS: turn left at the bakery for the new house
first directions after 488 ms, GPS switched on: 1
GPS: turn left at the bakery for the new house
second directions after 489 ms, GPS switched on: 1

The crew was ready with the GPS still off. The first request for directions paid for the GPS, and the second paid nothing: the same GPS, still on. Three rooms, three rolls of tape. Ask for GpsUnit directly instead, and the generated line becomes private val gpsUnit: GpsUnit = GpsUnitFactory.create(); the crew is then ready after 327 ms, with the GPS already on.

Laziness moves a cost; it doesn't remove one. The first caller who needs directions waits the 300 ms, perhaps at a worse moment than seven in the morning. And a cycle, a chain of "needs" that comes back to where it started, is still a cycle to our processor when one link is a Lazy. Nothing would actually be built twice there, but we chose to keep the check simple and strict.

Make a part lazy when it's expensive and not always needed. Build the rest with the plan.

The plan is fast now, and patient. But two claims about it still rest on our word: that the generated code uses no reflection, and that one edit doesn't redo everything. Let's check both.

try.expect: With Lazy, the crew is ready with GPS switched on: 0, the first directions arrive a little over 300 ms later with the GPS on, and the second directions take no time and switch nothing on again. Three rooms use tape rolls #1, #2 and #3. Asked for directly, the GPS is built with the crew: the first line reads about crew ready after 327 ms, GPS switched on: 1, and the directions cost nothing extra.

sections.h: Proof, not promises: no reflection in the generated code, and what one edit rebuilds
sections.html:
The first claim is that the generated code uses no reflection, a program inspecting its own classes while it runs. The lab doesn't take that on trust. One test reads every file KSP generated and fails if any of them reaches for reflection:

Java
// The same check in Java, with AssertJ, calling the Kotlin test helper
for (Map.Entry<String, String> file : run.getGenerated().entrySet()) {
    assertThat(file.getValue()).as(file.getKey() + " uses reflection")
            .doesNotContain("java.lang.reflect", "kotlin.reflect", "::class", "Class.forName", "javaClass", "getDeclared");
}
Kotlin
for ((path, text) in run.generated) {                          // every file KSP wrote
    assertThat(text).withFailMessage("$path uses reflection:\n$text")
        .doesNotContain("java.lang.reflect", "kotlin.reflect", "::class", "Class.forName", "javaClass", "getDeclared")
}

The race's class log agrees from the other side: no proxy classes, and not one annotation class loaded. That test is a cheap habit to keep. It fails on the day someone "just quickly" reads an annotation at run time.

The second claim is about the build. Incremental processing means KSP reprocesses only the files a change can affect. In the KSP track's picture, you repack one box, redo its card, and redo the master list. Let's watch it in lesson 3's source set. Build once with KSP's log switched on, add one comment line to Truck.kt, and build again:

./gradlew :injector:app:compileL03Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true
echo "// a comment, so the file's text changes" >> injector/app/src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Truck.kt
./gradlew :injector:app:compileL03Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true

KSP rewrites its logs on every run, in injector/app/build/kspCaches/l03/logs/. The second run's kspDirtySet.log said, shortened:

Modified
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Truck.kt
...
Affected By new syms
  build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Crew.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/MovingDayComponent.kt
...
Dirty:
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/RouteModule.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Crew.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Truck.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/MovingDayComponent.kt
  src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/MovingDay.kt

Dirty / All: 29.41%

And the end of kspSourceToOutputs.log:

All reprocessed outputs
  build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/CrewFactory.kt
  build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/TruckFactory.kt
  build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/MovingDayFactory.kt
  build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt

Five of the source set's seventeen files were dirty. Truck.kt is the one we touched. Crew.kt and MovingDayComponent.kt are listed as affected because the processors looked up Truck while reading them. Dirtiness then spreads: MovingDay.kt looked up Crew, so it joins, until no new dirty files appear. RouteModule.kt is dirty for another reason. It's one of the declared sources of the component, an aggregating output, and KSP files the component under <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>, its key for outputs that any change redoes. The figure draws the result. Three cards and the master list were redone; four cards came back from KSP's backups untouched: the driver's, the GPS's, the packer's and the tape roll's.

Two traps wait for anyone repeating this. touch Truck.kt changes nothing, because Gradle compares the text, not the date. And the build cache can restore old outputs after you undo an edit without running KSP at all, so make a fresh edit, or add --no-build-cache. One odd result, too: in three edit-and-build tries on this machine, one run reported Dirty / All: 100.00% with an empty Modified list, a full pass. KSP processes everything on a first build or after a failed one, and we didn't find what triggered this one; the next edit was incremental again.

Don't take a claim about generated code on trust. Test the text, and read the log.

That's the limit of the aggregating design, said plainly: the component is redone on every edit, however small. Here it's one short file. In a program with hundreds of classes it's one long file each time, which is a fair price for a plan that's always complete.

try.title: Read KSP's incremental log after one edit
steps: From labs/, run ./gradlew :injector:app:compileL03Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Open injector/app/build/kspCaches/l03/logs/kspDirtySet.log: what does Dirty / All say for this first build?

Add a comment line at the end of injector/app/src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Truck.kt and run the same command again. Read the Dirty: list and Dirty / All, then All reprocessed outputs in kspSourceToOutputs.log.
Now add a comment to Packer.kt instead and run once more. Before you look, predict which outputs are redone this time. Remove both comments when you're done.
try.expect: The first build with the log switched on reports Dirty / All: 100.00%: everything was processed. After the comment in Truck.kt, five files are dirty (Dirty / All: 29.41%), and the reprocessed outputs are CrewFactory.kt, TruckFactory.kt, MovingDayFactory.kt and GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt. For Packer.kt it's 29.41% again, with PackerFactory.kt, CrewFactory.kt, MovingDayFactory.kt and the component redone: the crew looked up Packer, and the moving day looked up Crew. If the log shows 100.00% with an empty Modified list, KSP did a full pass; make another edit and run again. If nothing ran at all, the build cache restored the outputs: make a fresh edit or add --no-build-cache.

sections.h: The real tools: Dagger and Hilt, kotlin-inject, and Koin
sections.html:
Everything in this capstone has full-sized relatives. Now that the idea is clear, here they are, each in a few plain sentences, as of November 2026.

Dagger generates component implementations and factories, the same two kinds of output as ours. Its KSP processor is dagger-compiler, and its docs say "Dagger's KSP support is stable as of Dagger 2.60+ and KSP 2.3.9+". Hilt, built on Dagger for Android phone apps, ships its own KSP processor, hilt-compiler, at the same version. Two warnings from Dagger's docs matter when you move a project over. Plugins written against Dagger's SPI, the interface its plug-ins use, must move to its new SPI. And "KSP processors are not able to resolve types generated by other Javac/KAPT processors". kotlinlang's list of supported libraries, on a page dated November 2026, still says "Dagger: Alpha" and "Hilt: In progress". Dagger's own docs are the ones to trust.

kotlin-inject is closer to what you wrote. It runs only on KSP, and its 0.9.0 release removed KSP1 support. In its README's words, "An implementation of this component will be generated for you". You reach it through a generated .create() extension, instead of a class name like our GeneratedMovingDayComponent.

Koin moved the other way. Its annotations used to go through a KSP processor that generated visible source files and extensions such as AppModule().module. Its docs now say "koin-ksp-compiler is deprecated and will be removed in a future Koin version". The annotations stay, and the Koin Compiler Plugin, koin-compiler-plugin, now processes them (1.2.3 on Maven Central, November 2026). They keep KSP only for projects that "can't move to Kotlin 2.3.20 or later yet". The plugin "replaces single<UserRepository>() (or the @Singleton class) with the equivalent of single { UserRepository(get(), get()) }" during compilation. That's a change to your own code. In the KSP track's picture, it's a job for the mover who repacks the box, not for the helper who can only add new cards. Each get() in that line asks Koin's container for an argument, so that part of the lookup still happens while the program runs.

Adding either of the first two to a real build is one line, as our app's processors are:

// build.gradle.kts of an app module: one of these, not both
dependencies {
    ksp("com.google.dagger:dagger-compiler:2.60.1")            // Dagger
    ksp("me.tatarka.inject:kotlin-inject-compiler-ksp:0.9.0")  // kotlin-inject
}

What you built has the same bones. There's a factory per class and a component per interface, checks fail the build on the exact line, and parts can be asked for lazily or through a provider. The real tools add years of cases you can now recognise when you meet them.

compare.title: A part that waits: Supplier in Java, Lazy in Kotlin

java.title: Truck.java
java.html: public class Truck { private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gps; @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { this.gps = gps; } public String directions() { return gps.get().directionsTo("the new house"); // builds once only if the Supplier remembers } } // a Supplier that remembers, written by hand static <T> Supplier<T> memoize(Supplier<T> make) { return new Supplier<>() { private volatile T value; public synchronized T get() { if (value == null) value = make.get(); return value; } }; }

kotlin.title: Truck.kt
kotlin.html: @Singleton class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) { fun directions(): String = gps.value.directionsTo("the new house") // builds once, then remembers } // the component's side: the standard library's lazy {}, SYNCHRONIZED by default private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() }

compare.note: Java's Supplier<T> only promises a get(): whether it builds once or every time is up to whoever wrote it, so a component that wants "once, on first use" has to wrap it, as memoize does. Kotlin's Lazy<T> makes the promise part of the type: .value builds on first use and returns the same object afterwards, and lazy { } is thread-safe by default. For a fresh object on every call, the two languages meet in the middle: Java's Supplier<TapeRoll> and Kotlin's () -> TapeRoll are both just functions with no parameters.

worked.title: Choose how each part asks for what it needs

steps.say: The driver is cheap to build and needed every day: ask for him directly. The component builds him with the plan and passes the object.
steps.code: class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver /* ... */) // generated: TruckFactory.create(driver, ...)

alt.html: @Inject public Truck(Driver driver /* ... */) { /* ... */ } // generated: TruckFactory.create(driver, ...)

steps.say: The GPS is slow to start and not needed on every day: ask for Lazy<GpsUnit>. Because it's a singleton asked for lazily, the component holds it in a Lazy and passes that.
steps.code: class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) // generated: private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() }

alt.html: @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { /* ... */ } // generated: private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gpsUnit = memoize(GpsUnitFactory::create);

steps.say: Tape runs out room by room: the packer asks for () -> TapeRoll and calls it once per room. TapeRoll has no @Singleton, so each call builds a new roll.
steps.code: class Packer @Inject constructor(private val newTape: () -> TapeRoll) // generated: PackerFactory.create({ newTapeRoll() })

alt.html: @Inject public Packer(Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape) { /* ... */ } // generated: PackerFactory.create(this::newTapeRoll)

steps.say: Check the choice with the app, not with your intuition: MovingDayApp prints when the crew is ready and when the GPS switched on. If a part is needed on every start anyway, Lazy only adds a lock and a box; ask for it directly.

lab.title: Lazy and provider requests
steps: Run the tests once. All four fail with l03 not done yet: unwrap Lazy<T> into (LAZY, T) .... Everything except two functions is the solution of lessons 1 and 2, as given code. The crew is in src/test/kotlin/workbench/injector/l03/MoveMateSources.kt, and its GpsUnit counts how often it was switched on.

Read: in Bindings.kt, write requestOf. Compare the type's qualified name with kotlin.Lazy and kotlin.Function0, and take the one type argument with type.arguments.singleOrNull()?.type?.resolve(). Anything else is a direct request for the type itself.
Write: in ComponentProcessor.kt, write reference(binding, kind, held) from the table in its KDoc. Then read heldLazily and componentFile, which are given, to see where your expressions end up.

Prove: run the tests until all four pass, including the one that scans every generated file for reflection. Then run ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l03.MovingDayAppKt -Pmine=l03 and check that the GPS stays off until the first directions.
Prove it again, from cold: run StartupRace with -Pmine=l03 and compare its class counts with this lesson's.
From memory: close the files and write the table of nine references (three kinds of request, three kinds of binding) on paper. Check it against your reference.
hints: For Lazy<GpsUnit>, type.arguments has one entry, and its type is a KSTypeReference: call resolve() on it.
A function type with no parameters is kotlin.Function0. Comparing that exact name also keeps (Int) -> Box, a Function1, out of the provider case.
CodeBlock.of("lazy { %N() }", name) writes lazy { newTapeRoll() }; %N takes the member name as a String.
If the GPS test sees GPS on before: 1, a lazily asked singleton is being built in the constructor. In reference, check binding.key in held before the plain singleton case.
lab.done: All four tests in LazyAndProvidersTest pass, and MovingDayApp with -Pmine=l03 prints GPS switched on: 0 until the first directions.

drill.title: Write a once-only box from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class Once<T>(make: () -> T) whose value calls make the first time and returns the same object after that, and is safe when two threads ask at the same moment. Then write the Java version as a Supplier<T>. (Kotlin's lazy { } is this, done for you; the memory model track explains why the field needs volatile.)

answer.html: class Once<T : Any>(private val make: () -> T) { @Volatile private var made: T? = null val value: T get() { made?.let { return it } // fast path: already built synchronized(this) { made?.let { return it } // look again with the lock held return make().also { made = it } // build once } } } val gps = Once { GpsUnit() } // nothing built yet println(gps.value === gps.value) // true: built on the first .value

alt.title: Once.java
alt.html: final class Once<T> implements Supplier<T> { private final Supplier<T> make; private volatile T made; Once(Supplier<T> make) { this.make = make; } @Override public T get() { T result = made; if (result != null) return result; // fast path: already built synchronized (this) { if (made == null) made = make.get(); // look again with the lock held, build once return made; } } }

recap: From cold, on a busy machine, the generated component wired the crew two to three times faster than the reflection container and the JVM run was shorter. The stable number was the class count: 817 against 1,059.
The generated path loaded no proxy classes and none of the annotation classes. A test that scans the generated text for reflection keeps it that way.
Lazy<T> builds once, on the first .value; () -> T gives one more on every call. The processor unwraps both to the type inside, so the graph checks don't change.
One comment in Truck.kt dirtied 5 of 17 files: the edited file, files that looked up its types, and the sources of the aggregating component, which is redone on every change.

Dagger and Hilt (stable on KSP since Dagger 2.60) and kotlin-inject generate component code as we did. Koin has moved its annotations from a KSP processor to a compiler plugin that rewrites your calls, which KSP can't do.
The limit: laziness moves a cost rather than removing it, and a generated plan can't change while the program runs.

explain.prompt: A teammate says reflection containers cost nothing worth measuring, because a call through one takes microseconds. Using the race and the GPS, explain what they're right about, what they're missing, and when Lazy helps.
explain.answer: They're right about the steady state: once wired, the second request took a few microseconds or less either way. What they're missing is the start. A reflection container reads every class's annotations and constructors on every start, so in our race it took two to three times as long to wire the same crew, the JVM run was tens of milliseconds longer, and it loaded about 240 more classes, including proxy classes the JDK generated to represent annotations. The generated component did that work once, in the build, and never even loaded the annotation classes. Fifty milliseconds hardly matters for a program that starts once a week, but it does for a tool or a test suite that starts often, and real programs have far more than eight classes. Lazy helps with a different cost: a part that's slow to build and not always needed, like the GPS. Asked for as Lazy, it's built on the first use instead of with the plan, so the crew is ready sooner. It doesn't remove the cost, it moves it to the first caller.

deeper.html:
Why count classes at all? Loading a class means finding its bytes, checking them and linking them, and every class costs the start a little. A count is also the honest number on a busy machine: it doesn't depend on what else is running. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class with its source, so you can tell your own classes from the JDK's and from classes made while the program ran, such as jdk.proxy2.$Proxy1.

Wiring generated at build time also suits the start-up tools of Part 4. A class data sharing archive or an AOT cache stores classes loaded from jars; classes defined while the program runs, such as dynamic proxies, can't be archived the same way, as the Part 4 capstone found. A generated plan leaves almost nothing to be made at run time, so more of the start can come from the archive.

Our component is eager except where you ask for Lazy. An eager plan is simple to read and fails fast: if a constructor throws, it throws when the component is created. A fully lazy plan, with every singleton in a lazy { }, would start faster still and build only what's used, but a broken constructor would then surface later, on first use. Both are reasonable; pick the failure time you'd rather have.

In KSP's incremental logs, kspLookupGraph.log lists what each reprocessed file looked up, so you can see exactly why Crew.kt became dirty when Truck.kt changed. With -Pksp.incremental.log.graph.origin= and a fully qualified name, KSP also writes a .dot file of the lookups around that symbol.
